hanshu.text:
The Book of Han (Hanshu, 漢書) was a family affair. Ban Biao, a prominent Han dynasty official, began compiling a supplement to Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji, 史記). He compiled many annals and biographies, but died in 54 AD with the work unfinished. His son, Ban Gu, took over the project, compiling most of the remaining chapters.

Several years into the project, the imperial court took notice of Ban Gu's private historical project. Concerned by this unauthorized private history of the dynasty, the court had Ban Gu arrested. Fortunately, Ban Gu's younger brother Ban Chao interceded. The court relented, released Ban Gu, and gave him a position in the imperial library. Eventually, Emperor Ming allowed him to continue his history of the Western Han.

Ban Gu continued his work on the history over the next few decades, while also boasting an impressive bureaucratic career. But in 92 AD, his fortune took another turn. The Dou family, relatives of the Dowager Empress, were purged en masse. Ban Gu was closely associated with the general Dou Xian, and was arrested as part of the general purge of Dou family associates. He died in prison, his historical work unfinished.

Finally, a third member of the Ban family took up the reins. Ban Gu's younger sister Ban Zhao, herself a gifted scholar, continued working on Hanshu for the next 19 years. She is traditionally credited with the chronological tables and the treatise on astronomy (with assistance from Ma Xu).

Hanshu began as a continuation of Sima Qian's Shiji, picking up the history where the Grand Historian had left off. It was this, the second book in the Twenty-Four Histories, that turned a single historical work into an established tradition. Subsequent dynasties after the Han would build on this established practice by writing the official history of the previous dynasty. This tradition would continue for well over a thousand years, even into the 20th century with the Draft History of Qing (Qingshigao, 清史稿).

This English edition of Hanshu is part of a new translation effort by translator and editor Garrett M. Petersen to create a comprehensive translation of all 24 official dynastic histories, as well as the Draft History of Qing (Qingshigao, 清史稿) and the Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance (Zizhi Tongjian, 資治通鑑). The effort is AI-assisted, with significant human editorial oversight and tuning. New technology has made it feasible to translate the nearly 40 million combined Chinese characters of these works into clear, readable English.

houhanshu.text:
The Book of Later Han (Houhanshu, 後漢書) tells the story of the Eastern Han dynasty, from Liu Xiu's restoration of Han rule after Wang Mang's collapse to the court struggles, frontier wars, factional purges, and regional breakdown that eventually led toward the Three Kingdoms period. It is the third work in the Twenty-Four Histories, continuing the tradition established by Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian and Ban Gu's Book of Han.

Fan Ye, writing during the Liu Song dynasty, compiled the imperial annals and biographies. The version transmitted today also incorporates the treatises from Sima Biao's continuation of Han history, giving the work its familiar shape as a comprehensive official history. Houhanshu preserves major accounts of the Guangwu restoration, the powerful consort clans and eunuch factions of the later Han court, the campaigns and diplomacy of the Western Regions, and the scholars, officials, generals, and critics who shaped the dynasty's political life.

This English edition of Houhanshu is part of a new translation effort by translator and editor Garrett M. Petersen to create a comprehensive translation of all 24 official dynastic histories, as well as the Draft History of Qing (Qingshigao, 清史稿) and the Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance (Zizhi Tongjian, 資治通鑑). sanguozhi.text:
The Book of Jin (Jinshu, 晉書) contains a detailed biography of Chen Shou, who authored the Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguo Zhi, 三國志). He was said to love books from a young age, becoming a clerk in the imperial library of Shu-Han. His early career was mired in controversy. When the eunuch Huang Hao dominated the Shu-Han court, Chen Shou refused to ingratiate himself with him, and was repeatedly demoted and censured. Later, when Chen Shou's father died, he himself fell ill, and he violated ritual by having a servant girl prepare his medicine. Others found out about this, and Chen Shou was disgraced. His reputation would not recover for several years, even outliving the Shu-Han dynasty, which was invaded and toppled by Wei dynasty forces.

Fortunately for Chen Shou, the Minister of Works Zhang Hua admired his talent. Zhang Hua declared him filial and incorrupt, appointed him as assistant drafter, and made him a magistrate. As assistant drafter, Chen Shou compiled the works of Zhuge Liang and presented them to the court. This earned him a promotion to drafter.

In this role, Chen Shou wrote the Records of the Three Kingdoms, consisting of 65 chapters containing biographies of important figures who shaped the history of the three kingdoms period. Chen Shou's contemporaries greatly admired his work. It was so good that, when Xiahou Zhan read Chen Shou's history, he tore up his own draft history of Wei and quit.

Chen Shou lived through the tail end of the Three Kingdoms period and wrote his history in the immediate aftermath, when sources were fresh and many key actors were still alive. Later, during the 5th century, Pei Songzhi revisited the work, adding commentary, annotations, and references to other sources, many of which are now lost. His annotations are marked 〈like this〉 in this edition. Pei Songzhi's additions increased Sanguo Zhi's value as a historical source.

In addition to being an important historical work, Sanguo Zhi became important through its influence on literature. Sanguo Zhi provided the historical foundation for the historical novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms by Luo Guanzhong during the early Ming dynasty. Romance adapts and embellishes Sanguo Zhi to create an epic drama full of intrigue, action, and larger-than-life characters. This novel was extremely influential on Chinese literature, becoming one of the Four Great Classical Novels of Chinese literature. Romance has spawned many adaptations in the modern day, from movies and TV shows to video games.

This English edition of Sanguo Zhi is part of a new translation effort by translator and editor Garrett M. Petersen to create a comprehensive translation of all 24 official dynastic histories, as well as the Draft History of Qing (Qingshigao, 清史稿) and the Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance (Zizhi Tongjian, 資治通鑑). shiji.text:
It was the year 99 BC, and a grim tension hung over the Han dynasty court, as word reached Chang'an of General Li Ling's defeat at the hands of the Xiongnu. When word reached Emperor Wu that Li Ling had not died in battle, but instead had surrendered to the Xiongnu, the emperor was furious. The one man in the Han court willing to defend Li Ling was his friend Sima Qian, a court historian. Emperor Wu had Sima Qian arrested, and he was given a choice: execution or castration.

Sima Qian accepted castration and imprisonment so that he could finish his life's work: The Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji, 史記), a massive, 130-chapter tome detailing the history of China from the ancient and semi-mythical Yellow Emperor to Sima Qian's own lifetime. The book was enormously influential on Chinese historiography, spawning a two-millennia-long tradition in which each subsequent dynasty would write the previous dynasty's official history, adopting the Grand Historian's structure and style.

This book is part of a new translation effort by translator and editor Garrett M. Petersen to create a comprehensive translation of all 24 official dynastic histories, as well as the Draft History of Qing (Qingshigao, 清史稿) and the Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance (Zizhi Tongjian, 資治通鑑). The effort is AI-assisted, with significant human editorial oversight and tuning. New technology has made it feasible to translate the nearly 40 million combined characters of these works into clear, readable English.
